name: Power Posing
description: The popular claim that briefly holding an expansive, 'high-power' body posture changes a person's hormone levels (raising testosterone, lowering cortisol) and increases their real-world risk tolerance and confidence -- one of psychology's most publicly famous claims (via a widely-viewed TED talk), and one of its most publicly disputed.
design_relevance_note: A direct, high-name-recognition test case for this project's own dialectic-verification mission: 'power posing changes your body chemistry' is exactly the kind of confidently-cited, TED-talk-popularized behavioral-science claim a design team might reach for in a wellness/confidence-building feature without knowing its central physiological claim specifically failed a better-powered replication.
myth_risk_note: One of the most publicly cited, least publicly corrected gaps between a famous popular-science claim and its actual replication record. The specific physiological/hormonal and behavioral risk-tolerance claims that made the original finding famous and TED-talk-worthy are the exact claims that failed to replicate in a better-powered direct test -- design or wellness content citing 'power posing changes your hormones' as settled science should be corrected to the much narrower, still-uncertain claim that survives: posture may affect how powerful you feel, not measurably your body chemistry or real-world risk-taking.
prevalence_note: Extremely well known publicly (Amy Cuddy's TED talk is one of the platform's most-viewed of all time) and still frequently cited in confidence-building, public-speaking, and wellness contexts, considerably more common in general awareness than in rigorous design-practice literature.

findings.description: A better-powered direct replication of the power-posing paradigm found postures did affect self-reported feelings of power, but found no evidence for effects on testosterone, cortisol, or behavioral risk tolerance — the original study's headline hormonal/behavioral claims specifically.
findings.source_title: Assessing the Robustness of Power Posing

applications.title: The original study's own co-author: 'I do not believe that power pose effects are real'
applications.description: Dana Carney, co-author (with Andy Yap and Amy Cuddy) of the original 2010 power-posing study, publicly stated that she no longer believes the effects reported in her own famous paper are real -- after a larger, better-powered direct replication (already the corpus's own primary science-tier evidence for this entry) failed to reproduce the hormonal and behavioral-risk-tolerance findings.
applications.ethical_note: A rare, notable case of a researcher publicly disavowing her own famous finding -- directly reinforces this graph's own dialectic-verification mission: a claim's continued popularity (Amy Cuddy's TED talk remains one of the platform's most-viewed) is fully independent of whether the scientists behind it still stand by it.
